meta.title: Inside One Chunk
meta.subtitle: 16 384 bytes, a 64-byte header, and then nothing but arrays — the stride is the entire point

views.label: The byte layout
views.note: Header first, cache-line aligned, then one contiguous array per component type.

views.label: One index, every array
views.note: An entity is not a struct. It is the same subscript into several unrelated arrays.

views.label: Why the stride wins
views.note: A job reads one array forward at a fixed stride. The hardware prefetcher can see that coming.

views.label: What decides capacity
views.note: Capacity is the buffer divided by the sum of the strides. Add a component and every chunk holds fewer entities.

cards.title: The numbers, from the source
items: kBufferOffset = 64, must be cache line aligned · Chunk.cs:343
The header is a fixed 24 serialized bytes inside that 64 · Chunk.cs:336

cards.title: Why an entity is not a struct
items: Entity 3's transform and entity 3's input are far apart in memory
They share only a subscript, and that subscript is the whole identity
A system that wants both reads two arrays in lockstep, both sequential
This is structure-of-arrays, chosen because it is what a prefetcher understands

cards.title: The consequence nobody warns you about
items: Adding a component changes the archetype, so it changes the chunk
That is a memcpy of every component of that entity into a different allocation
It also changes capacity, so a chunk holding 128 entities may now hold 113
This is why a structural change costs what it costs, and why you batch them

cards.title: What the job actually sees
items: One chunk, one archetype, one pass — no branch on type, no virtual call
Arrays it did not ask for are never touched, so they never enter cache
The tail of a partly full chunk is still walked as a range, never as a list
Chunk capacity is why job granularity is a chunk and not an entity
